name: Retinol & beta-carotene
job: Helps you see in the dark, keeps your skin and eyes healthy, and helps your body fight germs.
powers: Helps your eyes see in dim light
Keeps your skin and the lining of your nose and gut healthy
Helps your immune system fight germs
Helps your body make and repair cells
low: Trouble seeing when it gets dark
amount: Adults need about 700–900 mcg a day. One baked sweet potato covers more than a whole day's worth!
fun: The story goes that in World War II, Britain told everyone its pilots ate lots of carrots to see at night. The real secret was radar! Carrots do help your eyes, but they won't give you night vision.
warn: Too much vitamin A from supplements (not from carrots!) can hurt your liver and bones, and is risky during pregnancy. Beta-carotene from plants is safe. Eat a mountain of carrots and the worst that happens is your skin turns a little orange.
formsIntro: Vitamin A comes in two big groups: ready-made vitamin A from animal foods, and plant pigments your body turns into vitamin A.
forms: Ready-made ('preformed') vitamin A. Found in eggs, milk, cheese and fish.
The orange plant pigment your body turns into vitamin A. Carrots, sweet potatoes and mangoes are loaded with it.
Beta-carotene's cousins. Your body turns them into vitamin A too. Find them in pumpkin, papaya and tangerines.
The active forms your body makes from retinol. Retinal is the one that helps your eyes see in dim light.
Lookalikes! These carotenoids never become vitamin A, but they're still good for you.

subs.label: A
subs.name: Preformed vitamin A
subs.job: Vitamin A that's ready to use the moment you eat it. It comes from animal foods.
what: Comes from animal foods, mostly as retinyl esters, which your body turns into retinol
Your liver stores the extra for later
Your body turns it into retinal (for seeing in dim light) and retinoic acid (for growth and healthy skin)
subs.labelTip: Supplement labels usually say 'retinyl acetate' or 'retinyl palmitate'. Those are both preformed vitamin A.
subs.fun: Polar bear liver is so packed with vitamin A that eating it can make people seriously sick. Arctic explorers learned this the hard way!
subs.warn: This is the form that can build up to harmful levels from high-dose supplements. That's especially risky during pregnancy. Some acne medicines are made from vitamin A too, and they need a doctor's care.

subs.label: A
subs.name: Provitamin A carotenoids
subs.job: Colorful plant pigments that your body turns into vitamin A only when it needs it.
what: Beta-carotene is the big one. Alpha-carotene and beta-cryptoxanthin count too
Your gut converts them into vitamin A as needed
Some carotenoids, like lutein, zeaxanthin and lycopene, never become vitamin A, but they're still good for you
subs.labelTip: Look for 'beta-carotene' or 'mixed carotenoids'. Some multivitamins use a mix of beta-carotene and retinyl esters.
subs.fun: Eat LOTS of carrots and your skin can turn a little orange. It's harmless and fades when you cut back. Basically, you become a carrot. Temporarily.
subs.warn: In big studies, high-dose beta-carotene supplements raised lung cancer risk in smokers, so smokers should skip them. Beta-carotene from fruits and veggies is fine.

name: Thiamine
job: Turns the food you eat into fuel your body can actually use, especially carbs.
powers: Turns bread, rice and pasta into energy
Keeps your nerves sending messages properly
Supports a steady, happy heart
amount: Adults need about 1.1–1.2 mg a day. A bowl of fortified cereal can cover a big chunk of it.
fun: B1 was the first B vitamin ever discovered. Scientists noticed that people eating mostly polished white rice got sick, while people eating brown rice stayed healthy. The secret was hiding in the brown part!
warn: Drinking a lot of alcohol drains your B1. Your body would like a word.
formsIntro: B1 has one main form in food, and your body turns it into an active 'spark' form.
forms: The form found in food and most supplements.
The active form your body makes. It's the spark that helps turn carbs into energy.
A lab-made form of thiamine found in some supplements.

name: Riboflavin
job: Helps every cell make energy and keeps your skin, eyes and mouth in good shape.
powers: Powers energy-making inside your cells
Helps keep skin and eyes healthy
Helps other B vitamins do their jobs (team player!)
low: Cracks at the corners of your mouth
Itchy eyes that dislike bright light
amount: Adults need about 1.1–1.3 mg a day. Dairy, eggs and greens make that easy.
fun: Ever taken a multivitamin and then seen neon-yellow pee? Don't panic! That's B2 waving goodbye on its way out. Totally harmless.
warn: B2 hates sunlight, which breaks it down. That's one reason milk often comes in cartons you can't see through.
formsIntro: Riboflavin is the food form. Your body turns it into two helper molecules that do the real work.
forms: The form in food and supplements, and the reason multivitamins turn pee neon yellow.
An active helper made from riboflavin. It helps your cells make energy.
The other active helper. It powers energy-making and helps other B vitamins work.

name: Niacin
job: Helps turn food into energy and keeps your skin, gut and brain running smoothly.
powers: Helps hundreds of enzymes do their jobs
Supports healthy skin
Keeps digestion and nerves working well
low: Rough skin rash that gets worse in the sun
amount: Adults need about 14–16 mg a day. Your body can even make some of it by itself!
fun: Your body can build its own niacin from tryptophan, the protein piece famous (unfairly!) for making people sleepy after big holiday dinners.
warn: Big supplement doses can cause a 'niacin flush': red, hot, tingly skin. Don't take high doses unless your doctor says so.
formsIntro: Niacin has two main forms. They do the same job, but only one makes you blush!
forms: Found in food and supplements. Big doses cause the famous red, tingly 'niacin flush'.
Does the same job without the flush. You'll also spot it in lots of skin creams.
The active forms your body builds from niacin. They help hundreds of enzymes turn food into energy.
Not niacin itself, but your body can turn this protein piece into niacin.

name: Pantothenic acid
job: Helps your body break down fats, carbs and protein, and helps make some hormones.
powers: Releases energy from food
Helps build the fats your cells need
Helps make some important hormones
low: Very rare! Almost everyone gets enough
A 'burning feet' feeling (only in extreme cases)
amount: Adults need about 5 mg a day, and a normal diet usually delivers.
fun: 'Pantothen' is Greek for 'from everywhere'. B5 is in so many foods that running low is super rare.
warn: If you eat a mix of real foods, you're almost certainly fine. B5 is the chill one of the group.
formsIntro: Pantothenic acid is the food form. Your body turns it into coenzyme A, a helper used all over your body.
forms: The form found naturally in food.
The most common form in supplements.
The active form your body makes. It helps break down fats, carbs and protein.
Seen 'pro-vitamin B5' on a shampoo bottle? That's panthenol, used in hair and skin products.

name: Pyridoxine
job: Helps your body use protein and cooks up brain chemicals that affect mood and sleep.
powers: Helps make serotonin and dopamine, your mood messengers
Helps make melatonin (hello, sleep!)
Supports your immune system and red blood cells
amount: Adults need about 1.3–1.7 mg a day. One banana gives you roughly a quarter of that.
fun: B6 isn't just one thing. It's a family of six closely related compounds. Overachiever!
warn: More is NOT better. Taking very high-dose B6 supplements for a long time can cause numbness and nerve damage. B6 from food is safe.
formsIntro: 'Vitamin B6' is a team name for six closely related compounds: three main forms, each with a phosphate version.
forms: Found in plant foods. Also the most common form in supplements, as pyridoxine hydrochloride (HCl).
The active forms your body makes: pyridoxal 5'-phosphate and pyridoxamine 5'-phosphate. PLP is the busy one.

name: Biotin
job: Helps turn food into energy, and is famous (maybe too famous) for hair, skin and nails.
powers: Helps break down fats, carbs and protein
Supports healthy hair, skin and nails
Works with enzymes that build and burn fuel
low: Red, scaly rash around eyes, nose or mouth
amount: Adults need only about 30 mcg a day, and most people get plenty.
fun: Raw egg whites contain a protein that grabs biotin and won't let go. Cook your eggs and the problem disappears. Sorry, raw-egg smoothie fans!
warn: Biotin supplements can mess up some blood tests, including heart and thyroid tests. Tell your doctor if you take them. And unless you're actually low, the hair-growth claims are mostly hype.
formsIntro: Biotin keeps it simple. There's really just one form!
forms: The form in supplements and the form your body uses. Labels often say 'D-biotin'.
Biotin attached to protein in foods. Your body snips it free so it can use it.

name: Folate (folic acid)
job: Helps make and repair DNA and build brand-new cells, including red blood cells.
powers: Builds new, healthy cells
Helps make red blood cells
Very important before and during pregnancy for a baby's brain and spine
amount: Adults need about 400 mcg a day. Pregnant people need about 600 mcg.
fun: 'Folate' comes from the Latin word 'folium', meaning leaf. The name is literally telling you to eat your greens!
warn: Planning a pregnancy? Doctors usually recommend a folic acid supplement. Ask yours.
formsIntro: Folate comes in a few forms. One is natural, one is made in a lab, and one is in between.
forms: The natural form in leafy greens, beans and oranges. Your body absorbs about half of it.
The lab-made form in fortified bread, cereal and most supplements. Your body absorbs about 85% of it with food, even more on an empty stomach.
The form that travels in your blood. It's also sold in some supplements.

name: Cobalamin
job: Keeps your nerves healthy and helps make red blood cells and DNA.
powers: Protects nerves and supports memory
Helps make red blood cells
Teams up with folate (B9) to build DNA
low: Pins and needles in hands and feet
amount: Adults need just 2.4 mcg a day, which weighs less than a single grain of salt!
fun: B12 is the only vitamin with a metal inside it: cobalt! And your liver can store several years' worth.
warn: Vegans, vegetarians and adults over 50 are more likely to run low. Plants don't make B12, so fortified foods or a supplement may be needed. Ask your doctor.
formsIntro: B12 has four forms. Two are active in your body, and two are mostly found in supplements and shots.
forms: Lab-made and super stable, so it's the most common form in supplements and fortified foods. Your body converts it.
An active form. It's the main one in your blood.
The other active form. It works inside your cells' power plants (mitochondria).

name: Ascorbic acid
job: Builds collagen (your body's glue), helps heal cuts and keeps your immune system ready for action.
powers: Builds collagen, the glue for your skin, gums, blood vessels and bones
Helps cuts and scrapes heal
Supports your immune system
Helps your body soak up iron from plant foods
amount: Adults need about 75–90 mg a day (smokers need a bit more). One orange gets you most of the way. Half a cup of red bell pepper gets you all the way!
fun: Most animals make their own vitamin C, but humans can't. Neither can guinea pigs or fruit bats. Old-time sailors got sick on long trips until they packed limes, which is how British sailors got the nickname 'limeys'.
warn: Very high doses from supplements can cause stomach aches and diarrhea, and may raise the chance of kidney stones in some people. Fruits and veggies? Always fine. And sorry: for most people, vitamin C won't stop a cold, though it may make it a little shorter.
formsIntro: Vitamin C is mostly one molecule, but it comes in a few supplement styles.
forms: The natural form in fruits and veggies, and the most common supplement form.
Ascorbic acid paired with a mineral. They're gentler on the stomach and absorbed about the same.
The 'used-up' form after vitamin C fights damage. Your body can recycle it back.

name: Calciferol
job: Helps your body grab calcium from food to build strong bones and teeth.
powers: Helps your body absorb calcium for strong bones and teeth
Keeps your muscles working
Supports your immune system
low: Bone pain and soft bones (called osteomalacia in adults)
amount: Most people aged 1–70 need about 600 IU (15 mcg) a day, and adults over 70 need about 800 IU (20 mcg). Very few foods have much, so fortified foods help a lot.
fun: Your skin can make vitamin D from sunlight. That's why it's called the 'sunshine vitamin'. And it actually works more like a hormone than a regular vitamin. Fancy!
warn: Too much from supplements can build up and raise the calcium in your blood, causing nausea, weakness and kidney problems. Sunshine can't give you too much vitamin D, but it can give you sunburn, so wear sunscreen. Ask a doctor before taking high doses.
formsIntro: There are two main kinds of vitamin D, and your body converts both into an active hormone in two steps.
forms: The kind your skin makes from sunshine. Also in fish and egg yolks, and in most supplements.
Made by mushrooms and yeast in UV light. Used in some supplements and fortified foods.
Step 1: your liver makes this form. It's what doctors measure in a vitamin D blood test.
Step 2: your kidneys make this active hormone form. It's the one that helps you absorb calcium.

subs.label: D3
subs.name: Cholecalciferol
subs.job: The kind your skin makes from sunshine. It's also the most common kind in supplements.
what: Your skin makes it when sunlight (UVB rays) hits it
Found in animal foods like fatty fish and egg yolks
Your liver and kidneys turn it into the active form
subs.labelTip: Labels say 'vitamin D3' or 'cholecalciferol'. Most D3 is made from lanolin (the natural grease in sheep's wool). Looking for vegan? Find D3 made from lichen.
subs.fun: Window glass blocks the UVB rays your skin needs, so sitting in a sunny window won't make vitamin D. Your skin also makes less in winter and as you get older.
subs.warn: Too much from supplements can raise the calcium in your blood. Don't skip sunscreen to chase vitamin D. Ask a doctor before taking high doses.

subs.label: D2
subs.name: Ergocalciferol
subs.job: The plant-and-fungus kind of vitamin D, made by mushrooms and yeast in UV light.
what: Made when mushrooms or yeast get UV light
Used in some supplements, prescription vitamin D and fortified foods
Your body turns it into the active form, just like D3
subs.labelTip: Labels say 'vitamin D2' or 'ergocalciferol'. It's always vegan.
subs.fun: Mushrooms are little sunbathers! Mushrooms grown or set out in UV light make extra vitamin D.
subs.warn: Both kinds work, but studies suggest D3 raises blood vitamin D levels a bit more than D2. If a doctor prescribed vitamin D, follow their instructions.

name: Tocopherol
job: Protects your cells from damage, like a bodyguard for every cell in your body.
powers: Protects your cells from damage (it's an antioxidant)
Supports your immune system
Helps keep blood vessels open and blood flowing smoothly
amount: Adults need about 15 mg a day. A small handful (1 ounce) of sunflower seeds gives you about half!
fun: Its science name, tocopherol, comes from Greek words meaning 'to bring forth babies'. It was first discovered as something rats needed to have babies!
warn: High-dose supplements can raise the risk of bleeding, especially for people on blood-thinning medicines. Nuts and seeds? Totally fine.
formsIntro: Vitamin E is a family of eight! Only one form, alpha-tocopherol, counts toward your daily needs.
forms: The star. It's the only form your body uses to meet its vitamin E needs.
Alpha's siblings. Gamma-tocopherol is the most common kind in the American diet, thanks to soybean and corn oil.
Four more cousins, found in oils like palm and rice bran oil.
'd-alpha-tocopherol' is natural. 'dl-alpha-tocopherol' is lab-made and only about half as strong per milligram.

subs.label: E
subs.name: Alpha, beta, gamma & delta
subs.job: Four forms of vitamin E, and alpha-tocopherol is the one your body keeps.
what: Come in alpha, beta, gamma and delta forms
Your liver holds on to alpha-tocopherol and sends it around your body. It breaks the others down faster
Only alpha-tocopherol counts toward your daily 15 mg
subs.labelTip: 'd-alpha-tocopherol' is natural. 'dl-alpha-tocopherol' is lab-made and only about half as strong per milligram. 'Mixed tocopherols' means all four.
subs.fun: Food makers add tocopherols to oils and snacks to stop them going stale. If you see it on an ingredient list, it's working as a natural preservative!
subs.warn: High-dose vitamin E supplements can raise the risk of bleeding, especially for people on blood thinners. Nuts and seeds are totally fine.

subs.label: E
subs.name: Alpha, beta, gamma & delta
subs.job: Four lesser-known forms of vitamin E, found mainly in certain oils and grains.
what: Come in alpha, beta, gamma and delta forms, just like tocopherols
Shaped a little differently: their 'tail' is bendier
They don't count toward your daily vitamin E needs. Scientists are still studying what they do
subs.labelTip: Usually sold as 'tocotrienol complex', often made from palm or annatto.
subs.fun: Tocotrienols were first found in 1964, in rubber tree sap. That's more than 40 years after vitamin E was discovered. Fashionably late!
subs.warn: Research on tocotrienol supplements is still early. Like other vitamin E supplements, they may affect bleeding, so check with a doctor first.

name: Phylloquinone & menaquinone
job: Helps your blood clot so cuts stop bleeding, and helps keep your bones strong.
powers: Helps blood clot so cuts stop bleeding
Helps build strong bones
Teams up with calcium and vitamin D
low: Bleeding that's slow to stop, like nosebleeds or bleeding gums
amount: Adult men need about 120 mcg a day and women about 90 mcg. Half a cup of cooked spinach or collard greens can cover several days' worth.
fun: The 'K' comes from the German word 'Koagulation' (clotting). Babies are born with very little, so most newborns get a vitamin K shot right after birth.
warn: Taking a blood thinner like warfarin? Don't stop eating greens. Just keep the amount you eat steady from day to day, and talk to your doctor before making big changes.
formsIntro: Vitamin K has two natural forms: K1 from plants, and K2 from bacteria and animal foods.
forms: The main form in food, mostly from green leafy veggies.
A whole series, MK-4 through MK-13. Found in fermented foods, cheese and eggs, and made by the bacteria in your gut.
A K2 form your body makes from K1.
A K2 form packed into natto, a sticky fermented soybean dish from Japan.
A lab-made form. It's no longer used in supplements because it harmed liver cells in lab studies.

subs.label: K1
subs.name: Phylloquinone
subs.job: The main kind of vitamin K in food, made by green plants.
what: Made by green plants as part of photosynthesis
Your liver uses it to make the proteins that help blood clot
Your body turns some of it into K2 (MK-4)
subs.labelTip: Labels say 'phylloquinone' or 'phytonadione'. Phytonadione is the medicine name, and it's the kind in the vitamin K shot newborns get.
subs.fun: Vitamin K is fat-soluble, so a drizzle of oil on your greens helps you absorb more of it. Salad dressing, you're actually helping!
subs.warn: On a blood thinner like warfarin? Keep the amount of leafy greens you eat steady from day to day, and talk to your doctor before making big changes.

subs.label: K2
subs.name: Menaquinones
subs.job: A family of vitamin K forms made by bacteria. Find them in fermented foods and some animal foods.
what: Named MK-4 through MK-13, after the length of their tail
MK-4 comes from animal foods and is made by your body from K1. Longer ones like MK-7 come from bacteria, including the ones in your gut
The longer forms stay in your blood longer than K1
subs.fun: Natto has more vitamin K2 than almost any other food: about 850 mcg in a 3-ounce serving! It's also famous for being super sticky and stringy.
subs.warn: K2 supplements can also interfere with blood thinners like warfarin. Check with your doctor before taking them.
